query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning–based predictive approach that explicitly incorporates descriptors for atomic‐level force‐constant fluctuations and local chemical disorder will more accurately identify high-entropy alloy compositions with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity than conventional methods based solely on mass and size parameters.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy alloys (e.g., alloys similar to FeCoCrMnNi) produced by conventional melting and homogenization methods.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an ML model trained on descriptors that include not only elemental mass and size differences but also parameters reflecting force-constant variability and local bond fluctuations. Use the model to screen the compositional space and then synthesize the predicted HEA candidates.
generation.conditions: Samples are synthesized under controlled conditions ensuring phase homogeneity and then tested at room to moderate temperatures. Inelastic neutron or high-resolution X-ray scattering experiments are performed to probe phonon dispersions and scattering, and complementary thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via time-domain thermoreflectance) are carried out.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical disorder and force-constant fluctuations within the crystal lattice, which enhance phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: In multi-principal-element alloys, enhanced local disorder leads to larger fluctuations in the interatomic force constants. This in turn scatters heat-carrying phonons more effectively, reducing phonon lifetime and lowering lattice thermal conductivity. An ML model that uses descriptors capturing these fluctuations can therefore identify compositions exhibiting this enhanced scattering, outperforming approaches that consider only mass and size effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs identified by this predictive approach will exhibit lattice thermal conductivities approximately 20–30% lower than those predicted by conventional descriptor-based models that omit force-constant disorder, reflecting a significant improvement in prediction accuracy.
generation.baseline: Current predictive methods that rely on traditional descriptors such as average elemental mass and size mismatch, which have had limited success in differentiating HEAs with very low thermal conductivity.
generation.boundary: The improved predictive capability should apply primarily to single-phase, chemically homogeneous HEAs. In systems where significant phase separation or inhomogeneity occurs, or where additional scattering mechanisms (e.g., from precipitates or oxidation) dominate, the approach may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy (e.g., the exact percentage reduction in prediction error) depends on the availability and quality of training data for the force-constant fluctuations. Variations in synthesis and measurement conditions may also affect the observed outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Use the ML model to select a set of HEA compositions predicted to have significantly reduced lattice thermal conductivity. Synthesize these alloys under identical processing conditions ensuring single-phase microstructures. Characterize the phonon dispersion and scattering parameters via inelastic neutron scattering and measure the lattice thermal conductivity using a transient thermoreflectance method across a relevant temperature range.
measurements: Phonon dispersion curves and attenuation (via inelastic neutron or high-resolution X-ray scattering)
Lattice thermal conductivity (via time-domain thermoreflectance or equivalent technique)
Microstructural analysis (via SEM or TEM confirming phase homogeneity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivities of the predicted alloys are not at least 20% lower than those predicted by conventional models or if the phonon scattering data do not show enhanced force-constant fluctuations as anticipated, then the hypothesis that incorporating such descriptors improves prediction accuracy is falsified.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. If this is unexpected from Mu’s theory, which would predict increased force-constant fluctuations due to the larger variability of random environments of a given atomic pair, it explains recent experimental reports on comparable phonon lattice thermal conductivities in our HEA and FeNi
